violations.name: Letter grade card not posted, hidden or removed
violations.law: 24 RCNY §23-07; NYC Health Code §81.51; 24 RCNY Chapter 23, Appendix 23-C, codes 20-05, 20-06, 20-07
violations.note: Appendix 23-C: code 20-06 grade card not posted $500 (default $1,000); code 20-05 card not conspicuously posted or not visible to passersby $500 (default $1,000); code 20-07 grade card removed, destroyed or defaced $1,000 (default $2,000). The game uses the removal row: $1,000, or $2,000 if the summons is ignored. Numbers read in search excerpts of the rule text; the page itself could not be opened from this session.

violations.name: Hand-wash sink blocked, without hot water, soap or paper towels
violations.law: NYC Health Code §81.21; 24 RCNY Chapter 23, Appendix 23-C, code 05D
violations.note: Appendix 23-A, code 05D (critical): no hand wash facility in or next to the toilet room or within 25 feet of food preparation, facility blocked or used for something else, no hot and cold running water, no soap or drying device: 10 points at condition IV and 28 points at condition V, which alone is a C. Appendix 23-C penalty $300 to $350. The one closure day is my estimate: with no hot water in the shop at all the inspector cannot let service continue until it is back.

violations.name: Ready-to-eat food handled with bare hands
violations.law: NYC Health Code §81.07; 24 RCNY Chapter 23, Appendix 23-C, code 04C
violations.note: Penalty schedule, code 04C, a public health hazard: food worker does not use a utensil or other barrier to avoid bare hand contact with ready-to-eat food: $250, $300, $350, $400 and $600 by condition level, the level set by the number of workers doing it. A pastry picked up without tongs, tissue or gloves counts. Game formula: $300 in the first month up to $600.

violations.name: Dogs or other live animals inside the shop
violations.law: NYC Health Code §81.25; 24 RCNY Chapter 23, Appendix 23-C, code 04O
violations.note: Penalty schedule, code 04O (critical): live animal other than fish in a tank or a service animal present in the food or non-food areas: $200, $200, $250, $300, $350 by the number of animals. Service animals must be let in; a pet dog may sit only at outdoor tables under the city's dogs-in-outdoor-dining rules.

violations.name: Refusing or obstructing a health inspection
violations.law: NYC Health Code §3.15(a); 24 RCNY Chapter 23, Appendix 23-C, code 07A
violations.note: Appendix 23-C, code 07A: obstruction of Department personnel $1,000 (seen in the rule excerpt). The $2,000 ceiling is my assumption that the default penalty doubles, as it does for the grade card rows; the default figure was not in the excerpt. Locking the door, hiding the kitchen or keeping the inspector waiting all count, and the inspection then happens anyway.

violations.name: Fire extinguishers missing, blocked or not serviced
violations.law: NYC Fire Code FC 906; 3 RCNY §109-03, Appendix A, Violation Category 1
violations.note: FDNY penalty schedule, Violation Category 1 (portable fire extinguishers and fire hoses): first violation $600, mitigated to $300 if you appear at the hearing and prove it was fixed by the hearing date, $1,000 if you default; second violation $1,500 (mitigated $750, maximum $5,000). FDNY's portable extinguisher flyer: extinguishers must be serviced yearly by a company holding an FDNY certificate (W-96) and checked visually every month, with the tag dated and initialed. Fire Code section number cited from memory.

violations.name: Exit door or exit path blocked
violations.law: NYC Fire Code FC 1031 (maintenance of means of egress); 3 RCNY §109-03, Appendix A, Violation Category 9
violations.note: FDNY penalty schedule, Violation Category 9 (rooftop access and means of egress): first violation $950, mitigated $475, $1,000 on default; second violation $2,375 (mitigated $1,185, maximum $5,000). Milk crates, cup cases and the mop bucket in the back corridor are the usual cause in a small shop. Fire Code section number cited from memory.

violations.name: Overcrowding: more people than the space is approved for
violations.law: NYC Fire Code FC 107.6; NYC Administrative Code §28-117.1 (Place of Assembly Certificate of Operation for 75 or more people); 3 RCNY §109-03, Appendix A, Violation Category 10
violations.note: FDNY penalty schedule, Violation Category 10 (overcrowding): first violation $950, mitigated $475, $1,000 on default; second violation $2,375 (mitigated $1,185, maximum $5,000). The game charges $950 the first time and caps at the second-violation amount. A room that gathers 75 or more people needs a Place of Assembly Certificate of Operation (NYC Business restaurant page); a small cafe has none, so a packed open-mic night breaks the rule. Fire Code and Administrative Code section numbers cited from memory. Fire officers can also order the room emptied on the spot.

violations.name: Candles or open flame without an FDNY permit
violations.law: NYC Fire Code FC 105.6, FC 308; 3 RCNY §109-03, Appendix A, Violation Category 3
violations.note: FDNY Restaurant Fire Safety Guide (2026 edition): open flames such as candles in a dining area need an FDNY permit; the yearly inspection fee is $210. FDNY penalty schedule, Violation Category 3 (permits): first violation $700, mitigated $350, $1,000 on default; second violation $1,750. Fire Code section numbers cited from memory.

violations.name: Construction, plumbing or electrical work without a Buildings permit
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §28-105.1, §28-213.1 (civil penalty for work without a permit)
violations.note: Department of Buildings: for buildings other than one- and two-family homes the civil penalty for work without a permit is 21 times the permit fee, never less than $6,000 and never more than $15,000; the inspector also posts a Stop Work Order, and working through it costs $6,000 for the first offense. The work must then be legalized with filed plans, so the permit is paid for anyway. Numbers read in search excerpts of DOB pages and service notices; the section numbers are cited from memory.

violations.name: Working through a Stop Work Order
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §28-207.2 (stop work orders)
violations.criminal: Violating a Stop Work Order is also a misdemeanor under the Administrative Code (§28-207.2, cited from memory).
violations.note: Seen at the Department of Buildings Stop Work Order page: first offense $6,000. The amount for later offenses was not in the excerpt (from memory it is $12,000); the game charges $6,000 for every month the work goes on. The order stays on the door until the permit exists and the penalties are paid.

violations.name: Sidewalk and gutter not swept
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §16-118(2)
violations.note: DSNY guide for businesses, Avoiding Common Sanitation Violations: failure to clean the sidewalk $100 to $300; failure to clean 18 inches from the curb into the street $100 to $300 (two separate tickets). Sanitation agents may ticket a commercial property only during two one-hour periods a day, printed on the DSNY notice for the block. Game formula: $100 the first month, up to $300.

violations.name: Shop trash in public litter baskets, no private carter
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §16-116 (commercial waste must go to a licensed private carter), §16-120(c) and (e)
violations.note: DSNY guide for businesses: every business must hire a private carter and post its decal; business waste may never be placed in or beside the corner litter baskets; fine $100 to $300 (Administrative Code §16-120(c) and (e)). Game formula: $100 plus $100 for each further month, capped at $300 per ticket. Agents open the bags and look for mail and receipts with the shop's name. §16-116 cited from memory.

violations.name: A-frame sign or merchandise blocking the sidewalk
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §16-118 and §19-136 (sidewalk obstructions)
violations.note: NYC311: a sandwich or A-frame sign may not reach more than 3 feet into the sidewalk from the building. The Sanitation Department told the Midtown Gazette in 2015 that the fine is $100 for a first sign violation and up to $300 after that; a New York coffee shop was reported fined $300 for a sidewalk sign. I did not find the current penalty row, so the amounts are from press reports. Section numbers cited from memory.

violations.name: Backflow prevention device not tested this year
violations.law: 15 RCNY §20-04(e); NYS Sanitary Code 10 NYCRR §5-1.31
violations.note: OATH water penalty schedule: failure to submit the annual backflow test report (15 RCNY §20-04(e)) $500, mitigated to $50 if the report is filed before the first hearing date, $1,000 maximum. The device on the water service must be tested once a year by a state-certified tester and the report sent to the Department of Environmental Protection, which finds missing reports from its own records. In 2018 the city wrote 8,780 violations for missing reports (Public Advocate). The state code section is cited from memory.

violations.name: Music too loud for the neighbors
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §24-231(a) (commercial music); 15 RCNY §47-02 (Noise Code penalty schedule)
violations.note: Noise Code: music from a commercial establishment may not exceed 42 dB(A) measured inside a neighbor's home. Penalty schedule for §24-231(a): $2,000 for a first offense, $4,000 for a second, $6,000 for a third; maximums $8,000, $16,000 and $24,000. A Department of Environmental Protection form lets a first offender bring the $2,000 down to $0 by admitting the violation and filing proof of correction from a noise consultant by the deadline. Found through 311 complaints: an inspector takes a reading in the complainant's apartment.

violations.name: Card surcharge not shown in the posted price
violations.law: NY General Business Law §518
violations.note: General Business Law §518 as in force since February 11, 2024: a seller who adds a credit card surcharge must post the highest total price including the surcharge, and the surcharge may not be more than what the card processor charges the seller; civil penalty up to $500 per violation, enforced by local consumer agencies. A sign that says '3% fee on cards' next to a single menu price does not comply; two posted prices (cash and card) do. The rule covers credit cards, not debit cards.

violations.name: Required health signs and posters missing
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §17-172 (choking first aid poster), §17-188 (resuscitation equipment); NYC Health Code §81.21(c) (wash hands sign); NYC Health Code Article 81 (Healthy Eating Information poster)
violations.note: Seen at NYC Health: restaurants must post the choking first aid poster, the CPR equipment notice, the wash-hands sign, the no smoking sign and the Healthy Eating Information poster (alcohol and pregnancy warning if alcohol is served); the city gives all of them away free through 311. Seen: $200 for a missing Healthy Eating poster (NYC Health FAQ) and $200 for a missing wash-hands sign (2022 rule notice). The $200 per sign and the three-sign cap of $600 are my simplification; the penalty rows for the choking poster and the CPR kit were not in any excerpt I could read. Sign violations are unscored and many can be cured for $0 the first time (Local Law 80 of 2021). Section numbers 17-188 and 81.21(c) as cited by the sources.

violations.name: No food allergy notice on the menu or in the prep area
violations.law: NY Public Health Law §1356; NYC Administrative Code §17-195
violations.note: NYC Health: New York State requires restaurants to post a food allergies and intolerances sign where all food workers can see it, in the languages they speak, and to print an allergy statement on menus, online menus included; beginning January 2027 a restaurant that does not comply may receive a summons with a $100 fine. Public Health Law §1356 caps the civil penalty at $125 per violation. The fine is small; the real exposure is an allergic reaction with no notice on the wall (see extra.lawsuits).

violations.name: Trash set out in bags, at the wrong time, or without a lidded bin
violations.law: 16 RCNY §1-02.1 (commercial containerization); NYC Administrative Code §16-120
violations.note: Sanitation Department: since March 1, 2024 every business must put trash at the curb in bins with secure lids; $50 for a first offense, $100 for a second, $200 for every one after. DSNY business set-out rules: bins go out one hour before closing or after 8 PM and must be back inside by the time the shop reopens. Game formula follows the three steps. The rule section number is cited from memory.

violations.name: Foam cups or containers
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §16-329
violations.note: Sanitation Department: single-use foam cups, plates, trays and clamshells have been banned since January 1, 2019; fines for each notice within 12 months are $150 for the first offense, $250 for the second and $500 for the third and later. The Health Department and DCWP inspectors can write the same violation.

violations.name: Plastic straws and utensils handed out without being asked
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §16-401 (plastic straws, Local Law 64 of 2021) and §16-402 (utensils, condiments and napkins only on request, Local Law 17 of 2023)
violations.note: NYC311 plastic straw rules: plastic straws only on request, with a sign at any self-serve station; $100 for a first violation, $200 for a second and $400 for a third within 12 months; enforced since November 1, 2022. Sanitation Department: utensils, condiment packets, napkins and extra containers may go into a takeout or delivery order only if the customer asks; $50, $150 and $250; violations written since July 1, 2024. The game uses the straw schedule. Section numbers and the local law number for utensils are cited from memory.

violations.name: Playing music without a public performance license
violations.law: 17 U.S.C. §§106(4), 501, 504(c); 17 U.S.C. §110(5)(B) (narrow exemption for radio and TV broadcasts in a food or drinking place under 3,750 sq ft)
violations.note: Not a government fine: the licensing societies (ASCAP, BMI, SESAC, GMR) send letters, then a field agent notes the songs played, then they sue in federal court. Copyright law sets statutory damages of $750 to $30,000 per song and up to $150,000 if willful, plus the other side's legal fees. Seen in press: four Connecticut judgments against restaurants averaged just over $3,600 a song; a Massachusetts bar paid $15,000 for five songs; a Connecticut restaurant $18,000 for nine. Game formula is my estimate: four songs at the $750 minimum ($3,000) plus $500 for each month the letters were ignored, capped at $30,000. A personal Spotify or Apple Music account is not licensed for a business; the radio exemption does not cover streaming.

violations.name: No sexual harassment policy or yearly training
violations.law: NY Labor Law §201-g, §218; NYC Administrative Code §8-107(29)
violations.note: Labor Law §201-g: every employer, whatever its size, must adopt a written sexual harassment prevention policy at least as strong as the state model and give every employee interactive training every year. The section sets no fine of its own. Game formula uses Labor Law §218 for violations other than unpaid wages, as quoted in the research notes: up to $1,000 for a first violation, $2,000 for a second, $3,000 for a third. The larger cost is in court: with no policy and no training an employer loses its main defense in a harassment claim.

violations.name: Storefront sign or awning installed without a permit
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §28-105.1, §28-213.1; NYC Zoning Resolution sign rules; Local Law 28 of 2019
violations.note: Seen at the Department of Buildings: a sign larger than 6 square feet needs a permit, and work without a permit on a commercial building is fined at 21 times the permit fee, never less than $6,000 and never more than $15,000. An appeals court upheld a $6,000 fine for an awning sign hung without a permit, and CBS reported $5,000 sign fines in 2018-2019 after a wave of 311 complaints against whole avenues. Local Law 28 of 2019 then froze penalties for business signs up to 150 sq ft and 1,200 lb; as I read it, the relief covers signs that already existed in February 2019, not a new sign, and I could not confirm whether DOB still applies it in 2026. Game formula: the $6,000 floor.

violations.name: CBD or another unapproved additive in drinks
violations.law: NYC Health Code §71.05 (adulterated food), §81.07
violations.note: Press reports from 2019 (CBS New York, Fox Business, Hemp Industry Daily): the Health Department barred restaurants and cafes from adding CBD to food or drinks, first embargoing the product on the shelf and, from October 1, 2019, writing fines of $200 to $650 by quantity; an earlier embargo hit activated charcoal. I did not find a 2026 city page confirming the amounts, so the range is from the press. Health Code section numbers cited from memory.

violations.name: Smoking or vaping allowed; no signs, no written policy
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §17-503, §17-508 (Smoke-Free Air Act)
violations.note: NYC Health: smoking and e-cigarette use are banned in restaurants, outdoor dining areas included; the owner must post no smoking and no vaping signs and keep a written smoking policy for staff. Penalties as described in the text of the 2002 act: $200 to $400 for a first violation, $500 to $1,000 for a second within 12 months, $1,000 to $2,000 for a third. I did not see the current penalty row, so the amounts are marked as an estimate. Section numbers cited from memory.

violations.name: Workers' rights poster not posted or handed out
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §32-102 (Local Law 161 of 2023)
violations.note: Law-firm alerts on Local Law 161 of 2023: since July 1, 2024 every NYC employer must post the city's 'Your Rights at Work' poster where staff can see it and give a copy to each worker, new hires on their first day; a first violation gets 30 days to cure, after that the civil penalty is $500. The statute itself was not opened, so this is marked as an estimate.

violations.name: Punishing a worker who complained
violations.law: NY Labor Law §215
violations.note: Labor Law §215: an employer may not fire, threaten or penalize a worker for complaining about pay or working conditions, to the boss or to the state. The Commissioner may assess a civil penalty of $1,000 to $10,000 (up to $20,000 with a prior violation in six years) and order reinstatement and lost pay; a court shall award liquidated damages of up to $20,000 to each worker. The worker has two years to sue (NYS DOL). Game formula: the $10,000 top of the first-violation penalty; with liquidated damages the total reaches $30,000. Cutting shifts or hours after a complaint counts.

violations.name: Job ad without a pay range
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §8-107(32); NY Labor Law §194-b
violations.note: NYC Human Rights Law: an employer with four or more workers must state the minimum and maximum pay in every job ad, a note in the window or an Instagram story included; the Commission can fine up to $250,000, but a first violation costs $0 if cured within 30 days. State Labor Law §194-b (in force since September 17, 2023): civil penalties up to $3,000. Game formula is my estimate: $1,000, capped at the state maximum. The city Commission also sends testers who answer ads.

violations.name: Step at the door, no ramp, website a screen reader cannot use
violations.law: Americans with Disabilities Act, Title III (42 U.S.C. §12182); NYC Administrative Code §8-107(4); NY Executive Law §296(2)
violations.note: Not a city fine: a private lawsuit. Seyfarth Shaw counted 8,667 federal ADA Title III lawsuits in 2025, of them 3,117 about websites, with New York the busiest state for website suits (1,021). NY1 reported an East Harlem restaurant sued over an 8-inch step with 43 alleged violations, and plaintiffs who each filed more than 100 suits; each suit asks for about $1,000 in damages plus the plaintiff's legal fees and an order to fix the barrier. The federal law gives no damages, but the city and state human rights laws do, and the loser pays the winner's lawyer. The $10,000 settlement-plus-lawyers figure and the $25,000 cap are my estimate: no public statistic of settlements exists because they are confidential. A complaint to the city Commission on Human Rights can instead end in a civil penalty of up to $125,000 (Administrative Code §8-126, cited from memory).

violations.name: Beer or wine sold to someone under 21
violations.law: NY Alcoholic Beverage Control Law §65, §17(3)
violations.criminal: The person who makes the sale can be arrested and charged with a misdemeanor.
violations.note: State Liquor Authority press releases on 2026 underage compliance checks: licensees charged with underage sales face civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation, with fines starting at $2,500 to $4,000 for a first offense; repeat offenders face suspension or revocation of the license. The Authority sends underage decoys with investigators. The licensee answers even if an employee made the sale and even if the buyer looked 21 or lied (SLA Handbook for Retail Licensees, July 2025). Applies only to a cafe that holds a beer and wine license. ABC Law section numbers cited from memory.

officials.name: Fire inspector
officials.realProcess: Fire inspectors and local firehouse companies walk through businesses unannounced and answer 311 complaints. They check extinguisher tags, exit paths, extension cords and permits, then write a violation order to fix it or a summons to the city tribunal (OATH), where the fine is halved if you prove the fix before the hearing.

officials.name: Buildings inspector
officials.realProcess: Almost always sent by a 311 complaint: a neighbor hears demolition or sees a dumpster and no permit in the window. The inspector posts a Stop Work Order and writes a summons to OATH. The work must be legalized with filed plans before the order is lifted.

officials.name: Sanitation enforcement agent
officials.realProcess: Agents walk commercial streets on a route. For dirty sidewalks they may ticket a shop only during two posted one-hour windows a day; for trash set out wrong, missing carter decals, foam cups and sidewalk obstructions they ticket at any time. Tickets are answered at OATH.

officials.name: Environmental inspector
officials.realProcess: Three separate units: sewer inspectors open the grease interceptor and ask for cleaning records; the cross-connection unit mails a notice when the yearly backflow test report is missing; noise inspectors answer 311 complaints and take a decibel reading inside the neighbor's home.

officials.name: Civil court (private lawsuits)
officials.agency: U.S. District Court (S.D.N.Y. and E.D.N.Y.) and New York State Supreme Court
officials.realProcess: Not an inspector: a private party's lawyer files a complaint and a process server hands you the summons. Small businesses almost always settle within months, because the law makes the loser pay the other side's legal fees and a defense costs more than the settlement.

officials.name: Human rights investigator
officials.realProcess: The Commission takes complaints from the public and runs its own tests: testers answer job ads and visit businesses. Small employers are usually offered an early resolution: fix it, train the staff and pay a set penalty. A contested case goes to the city tribunal (OATH).

officials.name: Liquor Authority investigator
officials.realProcess: Investigators send underage decoys into licensed places and watch the sale. Charges go to a hearing before the Authority, which can fine, suspend or revoke the license. Only a cafe with a beer and wine license ever meets them.

officials.name: Health inspector
officials.agency: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH)
officials.realProcess: Unannounced, at least once a year. The inspector walks the whole shop with a thermometer and a flashlight and scores each violation in points: under 14 is an A, and an A on the first visit also means no fines for the scored violations. With 14 or more, a second inspection comes about a month later and sets the grade; with 28 or more, inspectors keep coming about once a month. A hazard that cannot be fixed on the spot closes the shop. Fines are decided afterwards at the city tribunal (OATH).
